newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine's Kuchma accepts Lazarenko's resignation.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine's Kuchma accepts Lazarenko's resignation.

text.p: Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma said on Wednesday he had accepted Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko's resignation.
"The resignation is accepted, and there will be a decree later today," Kuchma told a news conference when asked to confirm whether Lazarenko had resigned.

Kuchma, speaking at a joint news conference with visiting Czech President Vaclav Havel, said a new candidate for prime minister would be named after consultations with parliament, which has to approve any appointment by a simple majority.
Kuchma is also bound by the constitution to re-appoint the entire cabinet of ministers if the prime minister resigns.
Presidential spokesman Dmytro Markov told reporters that consultations between presidential administration officials and parliamentary group leaders had already begun.

Kuchma, under pressure for months to dismiss Lazarenko, issued a decree on June 19 appointing his deputy Vasyl Durdynets acting prime minister, a move which was widely interpreted as a step towards removing Lazarenko from power completely.
Some Lazarenko aides said the wording of the original decree, which said Lazarenko, 44, was being replaced because of illness, was just a ploy and that he was being sacked.

Lazarenko took over as prime minister in May 1996 from Yevhen Marchuk, who was accused of mishandling the economy and of self-promotion. In turn, he was blamed in part for slow privatisation and failing to stamp out government corruption.
Western media have said that Lazarenko was behind Ukraine's biggest gas trader, the United Energy Systems of Ukraine, and alleged that he received $200 million in revenues.
Kuchma has slammed Lazarenko's goverment for failing to push through reforms and this year's budget, which did not receive parliament's approval until June 27.

Potential replacements for Lazarenko include Anatoly Kinakh, head of the Ukrainian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs, Serhiy Tyhypko, a deputy prime minister with an image as a youthful reformer and Olexander Tkachenko, a prominent leftist in the conservative-dominated parliament.
